prompt.context: Our client is the minister of education in Burma (Myanmar). School attendance rates have decreased approximately 10% over the past five years and the minister has been charged with reversing this trend. Through a combination of public funds, grants, and donations, the education budget has increased by an additional 150MM MMK (local currency) this year. The minister has hired McKinsey to help him allocate these funds to improve both the attendance and quality of the country's schools.
prompt.question: What are some areas you would first explore to determine why attendance rates have been decreasing?

clarifying_info.q: What is the total population of school-aged children?
How many students are currently attending school regularly?
How many months are students in school per year?
clarifying_info.a: An average of 10 months each year

exhibits.title: Voucher Pilot Results
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the results of a pilot voucher program tested on a sample set of schools. The x-axis is the voucher amount per student (1, 2, or 3 MMK) and the y-axis is the increase in attendance rate (percentage) for each voucher level.
exhibits.data: Three data points: $1 voucher = 20% increase in attendance among non-attending students; $2 voucher = 30% increase; $3 voucher = 35% increase

framework: Customer / Demographics: % of school-age population (is the school-age population shrinking?), child employment rates (families may send children to work), crime rates, drug usage rates
Infrastructure: transportation/access to schools, number of schools (closures), teacher and administration quality
School conditions: number and quality of teachers, student-to-teacher ratio, extracurricular and tutoring options, school lunch offerings

questions.prompt:
One idea is to incentivize families with a cash voucher per student, sent home monthly if the student meets an attendance goal. Given the pilot data (Exhibit 1) and the facts below, assess each voucher level: calculate the new attendance rate and total cost for $1, $2, and $3 vouchers.

Facts: Population of school-aged children = 10MM; current population regularly attending = 6MM; students are in school an average of 10 months per year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute additional students gained, new total attendance, new attendance rate, and total cost for each voucher level. Should identify $1 voucher as best ROI. Should also note pros and cons of the program.

math.setup: Current non-attending students = 10MM - 6MM = 4MM. Pilot data shows each voucher level increases attendance among non-attending students by a given percentage. Total cost = (new total attending) x (voucher amount) x 10 months.
steps: $1 voucher: Additional students = 20% x 4MM = 0.8MM; New attending = 6.8MM; New rate = 6.8/10 = 68% (8pp increase); Total cost = 6.8MM x $1 x 10 = $68MM
$2 voucher: Additional students = 30% x 4MM = 1.2MM; New attending = 7.2MM; New rate = 7.2/10 = 72% (12pp increase); Total cost = 7.2MM x $2 x 10 = $144MM
$3 voucher: Additional students = 35% x 4MM = 1.4MM; New attending = 7.4MM; New rate = 7.4/10 = 74% (14pp increase); Total cost = 7.4MM x $3 x 10 = $222MM
Cost per incremental student: $1 = $68MM/0.8MM = $85; $2 = $144MM/1.2MM = $120; $3 = $222MM/1.4MM = $159 — $1 voucher has lowest cost per incremental student
math.answer: $1 voucher yields 68% attendance rate (+8pp) at $68MM total cost — best ROI. $2 and $3 vouchers exceed or nearly exhaust the $150MM budget with diminishing incremental returns.

questions.prompt: McKinsey also piloted a school-level investment program: a one-time $10 investment per child currently attending school results in a 50% decrease in the truant population (assume the truant/non-truant proportion holds at the school level). Calculate the cost and impact of this program, and compare it to the $1 cash voucher.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total cost, new attendance level, new rate, and incremental improvement. Should conclude this program is clearly superior to the $1 voucher on both cost-effectiveness and quality dimensions.

math.setup: Currently attending = 6MM. Cost = 6MM x $10. Truants = 4MM. Reduction in truants = 50% x 4MM. New attending = 6MM + 2MM.
math.answer: School investment costs $60MM and raises attendance to 80% (+20pp), versus $68MM for +8pp with the $1 voucher. School investment is superior on both cost and impact, and also improves education quality.

brainstorming.prompt: What other additional areas would you consider for potential investments with the remaining budget?

categories.name: Classroom-related
ideas: Teacher salary increases or overtime pay for outreach
Additional school supplies or equipment (SMART boards, projectors)

categories.name: Non-classroom-related
ideas: Logistics improvements (bus services for children in remote areas)
Meal plans / school lunch programs for children living in poverty
Co-op programs where students earn household income while attending school

recommendation: Do not implement the $2 or $3 voucher programs — they are too expensive relative to the $150MM budget and have lower ROI
Prioritize the $10 per-student school investment program: costs $60MM, raises attendance by 20pp (60% to 80%), and improves education quality
With the remaining ~$90MM, make targeted investments in logistics (bus services), meal programs, teacher training, and outreach to address root causes of absenteeism
risks: Cash voucher program has long-term sustainability issues and does not improve education quality
School investment impact may vary across regions — truant proportion may differ by locality
Child employment and poverty are structural issues that require broader policy solutions beyond education budget
next_steps: Analyze remaining $90MM budget allocation across logistics, meals, teacher quality, and outreach
Pilot co-op or income-substitute programs to address child employment as a root cause
Track attendance rates quarterly to measure program effectiveness and adjust allocation
